slides.title: Thinking computationally before writing code
slides.subtitle: Architecture, explicit procedures, Python, and responsible generative-AI use
slides.teaching: Open with a familiar studio task and ask what would have to become explicit before a computer could perform part of it.

slides.title: Why code belongs in architectural thinking
slides.statement: Code makes a design procedure explicit, repeatable, and open to examination.
slides.supporting: A script does not replace judgment. It exposes inputs, assumptions, rules, and consequences so they can be tested and revised.
slides.teaching: Contrast a repeatable area calculation with a contextual design judgment. Ask which parts can be made explicit and which still require interpretation.

outcomes.head: Explain
outcomes.body: Describe a computational problem as inputs, process, outputs, and checks.

outcomes.head: Decompose
outcomes.body: Break an architectural question into smaller executable operations.

outcomes.head: Read
outcomes.body: Trace a short Python program from top to bottom.

outcomes.head: Evaluate
outcomes.body: Distinguish code correctness from model validity and responsible AI use.

slides.teaching: Frame these as abilities students will demonstrate today, not vocabulary to memorize.

items: Python expresses one step at a time
Testing and explanation keep the designer responsible
slides.teaching: Preview the cumulative argument: computational thinking precedes syntax, and evaluation follows execution.

slides.title: One architectural question, three levels of numerical reasoning

tiers.task: A rectangular room is 7.0 m × 5.0 m. Calculate its floor area.
A room is 8.5 m × 5.2 m. Apply a stated 15% material allowance.
From 420 m² gross area, remove 18% circulation, then fit twelve 24 m² studios. Find the surplus.

slides.teaching: Model the progression explicitly: one calculation, then a named assumption, then a multi-stage design argument. Students predict before seeing each check. Emphasize that the hard case is still a simplified program model.

slides.title: Every computational problem exposes four decisions

steps.label: INPUT
steps.head: What is known?
steps.body: Dimensions, counts, requirements, observations, material or site data.

steps.label: PROCESS
steps.head: What rules apply?
steps.body: Arithmetic, comparison, repetition, geometry, filtering, or search.

steps.label: OUTPUT
steps.head: What becomes visible?
steps.body: A quantity, warning, option set, drawing, chart, or recommendation.

steps.label: CHECK
steps.head: Why trust it?
steps.body: Units, known cases, boundary cases, provenance, and interpretation.

slides.teaching: Use a room-area example. Ask where the rectangular-room assumption belongs and how the result would be checked.

slides.title: An algorithm is a precise design procedure
slides.definition: A finite, ordered, unambiguous, executable, checkable procedure. Finite means it ends. Ordered means the steps run in sequence. Unambiguous means only one reading is possible. Executable means each step can actually be carried out. Checkable means the result can be verified afterwards.

example.head: Estimate floor finish
example.body:
1. Record net room dimensions.
2. Calculate floor area.
3. Apply a stated cutting allowance.
4. Report material required.
5. Check units and plausibility.

Five steps, in order, each one testable on its own.

slides.note: An algorithm is not the same thing as code. This one is written in English, and it is already precise enough to hand to another person.
slides.teaching: Have students identify which step is arithmetic and which step contains a project-dependent assumption. Step 3 is the judgment: the allowance is chosen, not derived.

slides.title: Decomposition makes broad questions executable
slides.definition: Breaking one broad question into smaller questions that can each be answered and checked on its own. You stop splitting when every remaining question has a single answer you could defend to a contractor or a reviewer.

example.head: How much finish material should be ordered for this floor?
example.body:
Which rooms are included?
How is each area calculated?
What unit is required?
What allowance is justified?
How are results checked and combined?

slides.note: Decomposition is not guessing the answer in smaller pieces. Each smaller question must be answerable from evidence you actually have.
slides.teaching: Ask pairs to decompose a daylight, egress, or program-area question into at least four smaller operations, then say which of the four they could not yet answer.

slides.title: Representation determines what code can express
slides.definition: Choosing how something becomes data — a number, a label, a condition, or a group — so that code can operate on it. A number holds a dimension or count. Text holds a material or room name. A Boolean records whether a rule passes. A collection holds several rooms or options at once.

example.head: A rectangular room becomes two numbers
example.body:
length_m and width_m support an area calculation.

They omit irregular edges, columns, wall thickness, tolerances, occupancy, and how the room is actually experienced.

The representation is what makes the calculation possible — and what limits it.

slides.note: Data is constructed evidence, not neutral fact. What a representation leaves out can matter as much as what it encodes.
slides.teaching: Emphasize that data is constructed evidence. Ask each pair to name one thing their chosen representation makes invisible.

slides.title: Abstraction creates power and a boundary
slides.statement: Abstraction means choosing what a model leaves out. Each omission adds power and sets a limit.
slides.supporting: The correct question is not only “Did the program run?” but also “Is this representation adequate for this decision?”
slides.teaching: Ask for one acceptable omission in a schematic calculation and one omission that would invalidate a recommendation.

slides.title: Automation and judgment have different jobs
slides.definition: Using code to perform a rule or calculation the same way, every time, without a person repeating it by hand. Good candidates are repeated calculations, consistent transformations, rule screening, searches across many options, and sorting or visualizing data.

example.head: The designer still owns
example.body:
Framing the question
Selecting the criteria
Checking data and assumptions
Interpreting context
Explaining the consequences

None of these become more correct by running faster.

slides.note: Speed and consistency are properties of execution. They are not evidence that a rule is relevant, complete, or fair.
slides.teaching: Stress that speed and consistency are properties of execution, not evidence of relevance or fairness.

slides.title: Generative AI requires an evidence trail

steps.label: ASK
steps.head: State the task
steps.body: Include known inputs, units, intended output, and constraints.

steps.label: TRACE
steps.head: Read every line
steps.body: Name each object, operation, dependency, and assumption.

steps.label: TEST
steps.head: Challenge the result
steps.body: Use a known answer, boundary case, and independent calculation.

steps.label: RECORD
steps.head: Document choices
steps.body: Note what was accepted, modified, rejected, and why.

slides.teaching: State the course rule: AI-assisted code is permitted, but unexplained or untested code is not acceptable.

slides.title: Python separates authoring, execution, and evidence

steps.label: AUTHOR
steps.head: Write statements
steps.body: Translate the intended procedure into explicit Python syntax.

steps.label: RUN
steps.head: Execute in order
steps.body: The interpreter (the program that runs your code) evaluates each statement and creates program state—the current value of every name.

steps.label: INSPECT
steps.head: Examine evidence
steps.body: Read values, types, output, warnings, errors, and figures.

slides.teaching: Introduce the interpreter and program state. Explain that later Spyder cells are checkpoints within one complete .py file.

slides.title: A Python script is an ordered sequence of instructions
slides.definition: A saved .py file holding one complete program. Python normally reads it from the first line to the last. Running the same script again, in the same order, reproduces the same result — which is exactly what makes a procedure repeatable rather than remembered.

example.head: week01a_area.py
example.body:
One file tells one coherent story: the inputs, the calculation, the printed result, and the comments that record the assumptions behind them.

You will save your first script in Meeting B.

slides.note: A script is not a conversation. Anything Python needs must already appear above the line that uses it.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slides 3–6. Show a .py file in the file browser so the extension registers as an ordinary saved document.

slides.title: One statement is one complete instruction
slides.definition: The smallest complete thing Python can carry out. A finished statement can create a value, bind a name, call a function, or produce output. Python completes one statement before it starts the next, which is why the order of the lines is part of the meaning.

example.head: area_m2 = length_m * width_m
example.body:
One line, one instruction. Python evaluates the right-hand side first, then binds the name on the left to that result.

A comment line and a blank line are not statements — Python skips both, so neither changes anything.

slides.note: Nothing is remembered between statements except the names you created. If a value was never assigned to a name, the next line cannot use it.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slides 3–6. Point out that a comment supports the human reader but is not executed.

slides.title: Commit to an answer before Python gives you one
slides.question: What does the second line print?
slides.why: print shows the value an expression produces, never the code that produced it and never the quotation marks.
slides.teaching: Take a show of hands on every option before revealing. Option C is what students expect if they think + always joins characters; option D is what the console echo looks like, not output.

slides.title: The first statement produces visible output
slides.explainBody: Python executes statements from top to bottom. Parentheses enclose the value sent to print. Quoted characters form text; 3 + 4 is evaluated before printing.
slides.teaching: Reveal the output only after the prediction vote. Ask why line one keeps its words and line two does not.

slides.title: A function call, and a note Python never runs

parts.label: Function name
parts.body: A procedure Python already knows how to carry out.

parts.label: The argument
parts.body: The one value handed in: a text literal, quotes included.

parts.label: Comment marker
parts.body: Everything after it on this line is ignored by Python.

parts.label: For the reader
parts.body: Says why the line exists. It is never executed.

slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slides 9–10 and 19. Read the line aloud: call print, on this one text value. A literal is a value written straight into the script; an argument is the value handed to a function. Then cover the code and ask what the comment was for.

slides.title: Comments preserve intent and assumptions
slides.code:
# Room dimensions are in meters
length_m = 6
width_m = 4

# Rectangular net floor area
print(length_m * width_m)
slides.explainBody: A comment begins with # and is ignored during execution. Useful comments record units, assumptions, reasoning, or a non-obvious choice—not punctuation already visible in the code.
slides.teaching: Compare the useful unit and geometry comments with an unhelpful comment such as 'multiply two numbers.' Delete a comment live to show that the output does not change.

slides.title: Whole numbers in does not mean a whole number out
slides.question: What appears in the console?
slides.why: Division always returns a decimal in Python, even when it divides evenly. 4 would be right in many languages.
slides.teaching: Option A is the most common answer and is correct in several other languages. Option D is the same division read backwards. Ask what the trailing .0 tells you about the kind of value, not the quantity.

slides.title: Expressions combine values with operators
slides.explainBody: Operators state the operation. The result can be printed, assigned to a name, compared, or used inside a larger expression. Parentheses make intended grouping visible.
slides.teaching: Ask students to name the operator and predict the value on each line: 5, 5, 20, 4.0, and 8. Only the division produces a decimal.

slides.title: Values have types before they have names
slides.definition: The category a value belongs to, which decides what you are allowed to do with it. Numbers calculate, text labels, and Booleans record a yes-or-no condition. Python assigns a type the moment a value is written, before any name is attached to it.

example.head: 42   3.5   'studio'   True
example.body:
42 is a whole number, 3.5 a decimal number, 'studio' text, and True a Boolean.

All four are literals: values written directly into the script rather than calculated from something else.

slides.note: 4 and '4' differ by two quotation marks and behave completely differently — one is a number, the other is text. Week 2 introduces a way to ask Python which one it holds.
slides.teaching: This is a preview for Week 2. Ask what operations make sense for a room name versus a room area.

slides.title: A variable gives a value a meaningful name
slides.definition: A name that refers to a value. The expression on the right of the equals sign is evaluated first; the equals sign then binds the name on the left to that result. A good name carries the architectural concept and the unit, so the line reads as a measurement rather than as algebra.

example.head: room_length_m = 6.0
example.body:
The name says what the number is and which unit it is in.

h = 6.0 stores exactly the same number and explains nothing at all to the next reader — including you, four weeks from now.

slides.exampleLabel: Name the concept and the unit
slides.note: The equals sign is assignment, not mathematical equality. It stores a result once; it does not declare a relationship Python will keep updating.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slide 19. Trace the values aloud and distinguish assignment from mathematical equality.

slides.title: An assignment stores whatever the expression produces

parts.label: The new name
parts.body: This name does not exist until the line runs.

parts.label: Assignment
parts.body: Bind the name on the left to the result on the right.

parts.label: First variable
parts.body: Python looks up the value it already holds, 6.0.

parts.label: The operator
parts.body: Two names and one operator make an expression.

parts.label: Second variable
parts.body: Looked up in exactly the same way; it holds 4.0.

slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slides 9–10 and 19. Cover the left side and ask what the right side is worth; then uncover and ask what changed in memory. Right side first, every time.

slides.title: Read Python as a small written language

steps.label: SCAN
steps.head: Start at the top
steps.body: Python reads the first line to the last, in written order. Nothing further down the page can change a line above it.

steps.label: NAME
steps.head: Label every part
steps.body: Which parts are literals, which are names, which is the operator, and which is a call to a function.

steps.label: EVALUATE
steps.head: Right side first
steps.body: Work out the whole expression on the right before the name on the left takes its new value.

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.head: Say the result aloud
steps.body: State the new value, the names that changed, and what print would show. Then run it and compare.

slides.teaching: Use one line such as area_m2 = length_m * width_m and have students name every syntactic role, then track which names change.

slides.title: Predict the printed value, not the arithmetic
slides.code:
room_length_m = 6.0
room_width_m = 4.0
area_m2 = room_length_m * room_width_m

print(area_m2)
slides.question: What exactly is printed?
slides.why: 6.0 and 4.0 are decimals, so the result is one too. print reports the value stored, not the name or its unit.
slides.teaching: Option A ignores the decimal inputs; option C is the belief that print echoes the name; option D assumes the unit in the variable name travels with the value. Python knows none of your units.

slides.title: Running the assignments creates program state
slides.code:
room_length_m = 6.0
room_width_m = 4.0
area_m2 = room_length_m * room_width_m

print(area_m2)
slides.explainBody: Each name is bound to one value: 6.0, 4.0, and 24.0. Change a name later and the earlier results do not recalculate themselves—program state is a record of what has already run.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slide 19. Name each variable and its value aloud before moving to the trace table.

slides.title: Trace state before running the program
slides.callout: A trace table records the state after each statement. It supports debugging and AI-code verification.
slides.teaching: Cover the final column and have students complete it before showing the answer.

slides.title: Three failures require different responses

left.head: Code-level failure
left.body:
Syntax error: Python cannot parse the statement.

Runtime error: execution reaches an impossible operation or missing name.

right.head: Model-level failure
right.body: The code runs, but units, assumptions, data, operations, or interpretation are wrong. This is often the more dangerous failure because the output may look plausible.

slides.teaching: Use a feet-versus-meters example to show that successful execution does not guarantee a meaningful result.

slides.title: Worked example: compare two rooms' area
slides.code:
gallery_name = 'Gallery'
gallery_length_m = 8.5
gallery_width_m = 5.2
gallery_area_m2 = gallery_length_m * gallery_width_m

studio_name = 'Studio'
studio_length_m = 6.0
studio_width_m = 5.0
studio_area_m2 = studio_length_m * studio_width_m

print(gallery_name, gallery_area_m2)
print(studio_name, studio_area_m2)
slides.explainBody: Two rooms, the same input-process-output rule applied to each, by hand — this is exactly the repetition a loop will remove in Week 3. Both models assume a rectangular room and omit wall thickness, columns, irregular boundaries, and measurement tolerance.
slides.teaching: Have students state input, process, output, check, and at least two omissions — then ask what would happen with ten rooms instead of two.

slides.title: An allowance is a multiplier, not an addition
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
waste_rate = 0.15

required_m2 = area_m2 * (1 + waste_rate)
print(required_m2)
slides.question: What number is printed?
slides.why: The parentheses add the 15% to 1 first, so 44.2 is scaled by 1.15. 6.63 is the allowance on its own.
slides.teaching: Option A multiplies by 0.15 and forgets the 1. Option B is what you get from 44.2 + 0.15, and also from dropping the parentheses. Option D assumes the result keeps one decimal like the input.

slides.title: ...continued: add the material allowance to both
slides.code:
waste_rate = 0.15
gallery_required_m2 = gallery_area_m2 * (1 + waste_rate)
studio_required_m2 = studio_area_m2 * (1 + waste_rate)
total_required_m2 = gallery_required_m2 + studio_required_m2

print(gallery_required_m2)
print(studio_required_m2)
print('Total required', total_required_m2)
slides.explainBody: 0.15 represents a 15% allowance, named once and reused for both rooms — that reuse is deliberate, not an accident. The numerical result still requires rounding, procurement knowledge, and evidence that the allowance suits the material and installation pattern.
slides.teaching: Students estimate first, then identify which value is empirical or project-dependent rather than mathematically necessary. Note that gallery_area_m2 and studio_area_m2 carry over from the previous cell — this is a live Spyder session, not a fresh script.

slides.title: Translate a design task into executable logic
slides.prompt: A rectangular gallery is 7 m by 5 m. Add an 8% material allowance.
steps: Write the input, process, output, and check in plain language.
Predict the area and approximate final quantity without Python.
Write four named Python assignments and one print statement.
Name one modeling limitation and one test case.
slides.teaching: Expected area: 7 × 5 = 35 m². With an 8% allowance: 35 × 1.08 = 37.8 m². Students should write four named assignments (for example length_m, width_m, area_m2, allowance_pct) and one print statement reporting the final quantity. Accept any reasonable modeling limitation (cutting waste, pattern matching, openings) and any sensible test case, such as confirming allowance_pct = 0 returns the base area.

slides.title: A program is an executable argument
takeaways: State inputs, process, outputs, and checks.
Represent only what the decision requires—and name the omissions.
Read Python sequentially and trace changing state.
Use generative AI only with explanation, testing, and an audit record.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students name one studio task suitable for computation and one part that remains a design judgment.
